newsitem.title: GERMANY: German union boss hits out at EMU cuts, UK opt-out.
newsitem.headline: German union boss hits out at EMU cuts, UK opt-out.

text.p: One of Germany's most senior trade union officials on Thursday attacked state spending cuts being made in the name of European monetary union and renewed calls for commitments to job creation within the Maastricht Treaty governing the project.

Ursula Engelen-Kefer, deputy head of the German Trade Union Federation (DGB), also said that if Britain did not sign up to the treaty's Social Chapter on workers' rights it should not be allowed to join the single currency even if it wanted to.

Engelen-Kefer's comments, published in an interview with the Handelsblatt newspaper, come after German finance minister Theo Waigel earlier this week said tax increases and welfare cuts could be the price that Germany has to pay to join EMU.
"We shall not however stand by and watch the Maastricht Treaty be abused as a justification for indiscriminate welfare cuts so that the little man has to pick up the bill for Maastricht," she said.
Engelen-Kefer warned that in the heightened climate of social conflict ahead of EMU, further unrest such as that involving Germany's miners, builders and steelworkers recently was possible.
"Nobody can know...what will be the event that breaks the camel's back. And we cannot guarantee that we shall be able to channel future protests," she added.
She insisted however that it was right that EMU should start as planned in 1999, even if it meant that the Maastricht economic criteria for entry were not precisely met.
Europe's trade unions and left-leaning political groups have so far been thwarted in efforts to have specific measures on employment included in the Maastricht Treaty.
The EU summit in Amsterdam this June is likely to be their last chance on the issue before membership of EMU is determined in early 1998.
Engelen-Kefer said upper thresholds for unemployment should be set, above which countries would be obliged to put special job creating measures into effect.

On Britain's continued opt-out on Maastricht's social chapter, which aims to ensure minimum workplace standards, Engelen-Kefer said that if Britain did not sign it, then it should not be allowed to enter EMU even if it wanted to.

She said the chapter should, rather than form part of the Maastricht Treaty, be included in the 40-year-old Treaty of Rome that created the European Union -- meaning that all EU members would have to abide by it whether insde EMU or not.
